• Imperial Reach: Military expeditions reached northern India while influence extended across much of the Deccan and peninsular India, effectively integrating the subcontinent’s geopolitical zones.
Architectural Synthesis

• Dravida-Deccan Fusion: Commissioned the Kailasanatha Temple (Ellora, Cave 16) under Krishna I, executing a pure Southern (Dravida) architectural plan directly into the solid basalt cliffs of the Deccan.
• Technical Mastery: Represented the peak of the rock-cut tradition, blending Southern structural plans with the grand scale of Deccan sculpture.
• Eclecticism: The Ellora complex integrated Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain monuments side-by-side, serving as a physical bridge between faiths.
Literary & Linguistic Fusion

• Bilingual Patronage: While patronizing Sanskrit as a pan-Indian scholarly language, the Rashtrakutas also aggressively promoted regional languages.
• Amoghavarsha I: Patronising/co-authoring the Kavirajamarga, the earliest surviving Kannada work on poetics and rhetoric.
• Vernacular Zenith: Supported the gems of Kannada literature (Pampa and Ponna) alongside traditional Sanskrit drama and philosophy.
Religious & Social Pluralism

• Patronage of Jainism: Major supporters of Digambara Jainism and scholars like Jinasena, even as Northern dynasties remained primarily Brahmanical.
• Vedic Legitimacy: Performed grand purificatory rituals like the Hiranyagarbha (executed by founder Dantidurga at Ujjain) to claim elite Kshatriya status while funding massive structural shrines for Shiva and Vishnu.
• Spiritual Harmony: Maintained peaceful coexistence among Brahmanism, Jainism, and Buddhism, reflecting a synthesis of diverse spiritual currents.

elements.text: 2. Art and Literature
The Rashtrakuta Dynasty (c. 753–982 CE) is celebrated for its monumental rock-cut architecture and its pivotal role in the development of Kannada and Sanskrit literature.

rows.text: Architecture
Monolithic Rock-Cut Temples: Mastered the feat of carving entire temple complexes out of single basalt rock formations.
Kailasanatha Temple (Ellora): An 8th-century structural wonder carved from top to bottom.

elements.text: Rock-Cut Cave Shrines: Constructed magnificent cave temples dedicated to Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain faiths.
Elephanta Caves was later supported by the Rashtrakuta dynasty
Dravidian Influence: Integrated Southern architectural styles (pyramidal vimanas, pillared halls) into the Deccan.
Jain Narayana Temple (Pattadakal).

rows.text: Art & Sculpture
Sculptural Grandeur: Produced dynamic, larger-than-life sculptures characterized by overwhelming energy and rhythmic movement.
Ravana Shaking Mount Kailasha (Ellora Cave 16); Dancing Shiva.
Literature
Kannada Language Zenith: Patronized the earliest major works in Kannada, establishing it as a key literary medium.
Kavirajamarga by Amoghavarsha I: The earliest Kannada work on poetics and grammar.

elements.text: Mural Traditions: Continued the tradition of mural paintings, specifically in religious cave settings.
Jain Cave Murals (Ellora) featuring celestial beings like Vidyadharas.
Sanskrit Patronage: Courts were hubs for Sanskrit poetry, drama, and philosophical treatises.
Prashnottara Ratnamalika (Amoghavarsha I); Nalachampu (Trivikrama).
Jain Literature: Supported eminent Jain scholars who compiled biographies of Tirthankaras.
Adipurana (Jinasena; later completed by Gunabhadra); Mahapurana (Gunabhadra).
Early Vernacular Masterpieces: Fostered the creative environments that produced the absolute foundations of classical Kannada poetry.
Pampa (Vikramarjuna Vijaya or Pampa Bharata) and Ponna (Santipurana).

The Rashtrakuta Dynasty declined in the 10th century due to the resurgence of the Western Chalukyas, led by Tailapa II. Despite their fall, they left a lasting legacy in art, architecture, and Indian history.
Pala Dynasty (8th -12th century)

The Pala Dynasty emerged in 750 CE under Gopala I, filling the power vacuum left after Harsha's death. Ruling Bengal-Bihar for over 400 years, they transformed the region into a thriving centre of Buddhist learning, establishing world-renowned institutions like Nalanda and Vikramashila universities while developing a distinctive artistic style that defined eastern Indian culture.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Pala period is the most significant phase in the history of Buddhism in India. Enumerate. (2020)
1. Art and Architecture of the Pala Dynasty (8th–12th Century CE)

rows.text: Architecture

• Mahaviharas: Massive brick-built monastic universities designed for Buddhist education.
• Pala-Sena Style: Development of a distinct local architectural idiom.
• Brick & Terracotta: Palas relied on baked bricks for construction & walls were ornamented with terracotta plaques depicting Hindu-Buddhist deities, daily life, and epics like the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
• Stone & Metal: Used black to grey basalt and chlorite stone for core structural elements like pillars and arched niches, celebrated for their highly intricate detailing and refined, polished finish.
• Influence: Their architectural footprint shaped later structures in the Bengal Sultanate, as well as monuments in Southeast Asia.

• Somapura Mahavihara: Located at Paharpur (Bangladesh); the largest Vihara in the subcontinent, featuring a unique, multi-tiered cruciform layout with numerous monastic cells.
• Vikramashila: Founded by Dharmapala; centered around a massive stupa flanked by 108 small shrines.
Sculpture

• Stone Mastery: High-yield, intricate detailing carved out of fine-grained black basalt (and grey chlorite) quarried from the Rajmahal hills.
• Metallurgical Excellence: Use of the lost-wax technique for devotional bronzes made from an eight-metal alloy.
• Stylistic Idiom: Slim, graceful figures in the tribhanga (triple-bent) posture on lotus pedestals.

• Nalanda & Kurkihar: Prolific centers for bronze casting, producing icons like Avalokiteshvara and Tara.
• Crowned Buddha: A specialized 10th-century metalwork style found in Bihar.
Painting

• Manuscript Art: Pioneered sophisticated palm-leaf painting using tempera (water-based pigments).
• Visual Technique: Figures sketched with black/red outlines over colored backgrounds with shading for 3D depth.
• Themes: Strictly Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist deities, mandalas, and scenes from Jataka tales.
• Vibrant Palette: Natural mineral/plant dyes providing bright reds, yellows, and indigos.
• Notable Manuscripts: Illustrated folios of the Astasahasrika-Prajnaparamita (8,000 verses on the Perfection of Wisdom).
Terracotta Art

• Monastery Ornamentation: Large decorative plaques used to embellish the exterior walls of mahaviharas.
• Diverse Themes: Blended Hindu-Buddhist deities with scenes from the epics (Ramayana/Mahabharata) and daily life.
• Somapura Plaques: Extensive collections found at Paharpur depicting Shiva, Buddha, and folk scenes.
Notable Artists

• Father-Son Duo: Dhiman and Vitapala (9th century) were the most celebrated masters of the era.
• Versatility: Renowned for their high-level mastery across painting, stone sculpture, and bronze casting.
• Royal Patronage: Actively supported by kings Dharmapala and Devapala.

elements.text: 2. Pala Literature

rows.text: Buddhist Writings
Patronised Buddhist scholars, producing sacred texts and philosophical commentaries → many translated from Sanskrit to Tibetan.

• Astasahasrika-Prajnaparamita (10th C): illustrated Buddhist scripture
• Tantric Buddhist Texts: Composed at Vikramashila University by scholars like Atisha Dipankara
Sanskrit Masterpieces
Kings sponsored Sanskrit works covering history, law, and poetry, creating a golden age of scholarship.
• Ramacharitam by Sandhyakar Nandi: Poetic biography of King Ramapala, simultaneously narrating the epic story of Ramayana and the historical crushing of the Kaivarta rebellion by King Ramapala.
Historical Records
Official inscriptions on copper plates and stone

• Nalanda Copperplate: King Devapala's donation to a Javanese king for monastery upkeep
• Bhagalpur Inscription: Construction of Shiva temples under royal orders

elements.text: 3. Palas' contribution to Buddhism
The Pala Dynasty (8th–12th century CE) was the most significant phase for Buddhism in early medieval India, transforming Bengal and Bihar into global centers of Buddhist culture and learning.

rows.text: Royal Patronage & Doctrine
Ardent patrons of Mahayana Buddhism; also oversaw the rise of Vajrayana (Tantric) Buddhism.
Rulers like Dharmapala were guided by spiritual preceptors such as the Buddhist scholar Haribhadra.
Institutional Centers
Built and maintained massive Mahaviharas (monastic universities) that served as international hubs for education and Tantric studies.

• Vikramashila University: Founded by Dharmapala.
• Somapura Mahavihara: Largest in the subcontinent with a unique cruciform layout.
Support for Nalanda
Sustained Nalanda University as a global seat of learning through land grants and fiscal support.
King Devapala granted five villages for a monastery at Nalanda at the request of the Sailendra King of Sumatra.
Buddhist Art & Metallurgy
Developed the Pala School of Art, characterized by technical finesse and spiritual serenity. Perfected the lost-wax technique for bronze casting.

• Nalanda Bronzes: Prolific production of devotional icons like Avalokiteshvara and Tara.
• Black Basalt Sculpture: Intricate stone carvings depicting life events of the Buddha.
Manuscript Painting
Pioneered palm-leaf painting using tempera, creating illustrated scriptures with vibrant natural pigments.
Notable works include the Astasahasrika-prajnaparamita and Pancharaksha Tara.
Literature & Scholarship
Patronized world-renowned scholars and the production of sacred texts, many translated from Sanskrit to Tibetan.
Home to eminent scholars like Atisha Dipankara and Tilopa.
Global Reach & Diplomacy
Acted as a cultural link between eastern India and kingdoms in Java, Sumatra, and Tibet .
Maintained strong ties with the Sailendra Dynasty of Southeast Asia and influenced Tibetan spiritual traditions in the 11th century.

elements.text: The Pala Dynasty established Bengal-Bihar as a centre of Buddhist learning and art, building monumental universities like Vikramashila and patronising revolutionary sculpture styles. Their 400-year rule ended when Vijayasena of the Sena Dynasty seized power, marking a Hindu revival in eastern India.
Rajput States (8th–12th century CE)

The Rajput states (8th–12th century CE) comprised numerous warrior clans that legitimized their political authority by claiming descent from mythical lineages such as Suryavansha (Solar), Chandravansha (Lunar), and, in later traditions, Agnikula (Fire-born). Rajput polity was characterized by a decentralized feudal (Samanta) system, strong clan loyalties, martial traditions, hereditary kingship, and ideals of honour reflected through practices such as Jauhar, Saka, and Kshatriya dharma.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. The sculptors filled the Chandella artform with resilient vigor and breadth of life.’ Elucidate. (2025)
1. Major Rajput Dynasties and Rulers
Major Rajput Dynasties and Rulers

rows.text: Tomaras
Anangapala Tomara; Capital: Dhillika (Delhi)
Strengthened Dhillika (Delhi) as an important political centre and constructed the fortified citadel of Lal Kot, the earliest extant fortification of Delhi.
Chauhans
Prithviraj III (Rai Pithora); Capital: Ajmer
Defeated the Ghurids in the First Battle of Tarain (1191) but lost the second (1192).
Gahadavala
Govindachandra; Capital: Kannauj
Successfully defended the kingdom against Ghaznavid incursions and consolidated power over the middle Gangetic plains. and patronized both Hinduism and Buddhism.
Solanki
Bhima I, Jayasimha Siddharaja; Capital: Anahilapataka
Also called Chalukyas of Gujarat, they commissioned the Modhera Sun Temple (Built by Bhima I);The Somnath Temple was rebuilt in phases by the Solanki rulers following Mahmud of Ghazni's raid.
Parmara
Raja Bhoja; Capital: Dhar
Raja Bhoja was a renowned scholar-king credited with works on architecture, poetics, grammar, medicine, astronomy, philosophy, and statecraft and founded Bhoj Shala.
Chandela
Yashovarman, Vidyadhara; Capital: Khajuraho
Elevated Central Indian Nagara style. The Kandariya Mahadeva Temple was most likely constructed during the reign of Vidyadhara, representing the zenith of Chandella temple architecture.

elements.text: 2. Art & Architecture of the Rajput Dynasties

The Rajput school of architecture is defined by defensive grandeur and residential elegance. It flourished between the 7th and 19th centuries in mediaeval India, spanning regions like Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Madhya Pradesh. It is defined by a brilliant synthesis of indigenous Hindu structural traditions with later Persian and Mughal influences, showcasing a deep martial spirit and reverence for the arts.
• Signature Features: Extensive use of Jharokhas (hanging balconies), Baoris, Burjs, Cornices designed to cast unique shadows.
• Military Architecture: Adaptation to rugged terrain with hilltop fortifications, such as those at Chittorgarh, Jaisalmer, and Kumbhalgarh [6:118, 16:108].
• Temple Styles:
 Maru-Gurjara (Solanki): Features decorated Torans and step-tanks (Suryakunds).
 Khajuraho (Nagara Style): Known for its Panchayatana layout, soaring shikharas, and intricate erotic sculptures.
• Urban Planning: Pioneered grid patterns and uniform facades, best exemplified by Jaipur City.
• Water Structures: Built elaborate stepwells like the Rani-ki-vav (Gujarat) for ritual and utility.
Chandella Art and Architecture

The Chandella Dynasty of Bundelkhand (ruling from Khajuraho) is renowned for elevating the Nagara style of temple architecture to its most sophisticated and dramatic form between the 10th and 12th centuries CE.
Temple Architecture

rows.text: Architectural Order
Developed a mature, localized variant of the North Indian Nagara style, distinguished by an intense vertical thrust (shikhara clustering) and lack of boundary walls.
Lakshmana Temple (dedicated to Vishnu).
Structural Plan
Preferred the Panchayatana layout, where a central main shrine is surrounded by four smaller subsidiary shrines at the corners of a high platform.
Vishwanatha Temple and Lakshmana Temple.
Temple Components
Temples consist of an Ardhamandapa (porch), Mandapa, Mahamandapa (greater hall), and the Garbhagriha (sanctum).
Kandariya Mahadeo Temple (dedicated to Shiva).
Verticality and Shikharas
Multi-tiered roofs rise progressively like a mountain range (Sringa). The main shikhara is surrounded by numerous miniature repeating towers (urushringas), terminating in an amalaka and kalasha.
Seen in Kandariya Mahadeo Temple (dedicated to Shiva).
Materials
Primarily used sandstone; however, earlier structures like the Chausanth Yogini used roughly-hewn granite.
Chausanth Yogini Temple (predates 10th century).
Decorative Sculptures
Renowned for extensive erotic sculptures (mithunas) and depictions of secular life, which were viewed as essential parts of the cosmic whole.
Laxman Temple (specifically the "Dance class" relief).

elements.text: Sculptures

The sculptures of the Chandella period (10th–12th century CE), centered primarily at Khajuraho, represent a peak of the North Indian Nagara tradition, known for their dynamic energy and technical sophistication.

rows.text: Dynamic Human Figures
Focuses on three-dimensional volume over flat relief. Marked by rhythmic poses (tribhanga) and a fluid sense of motion integrated into walls, plinths, and balconies.
Lakshmana & Kandariya Mahadeva Temples: Iconic dancing apsaras and surasundaris with deep undercutting.
Expressive Faces and Emotions
Conveys deep emotional realism (devotion, desire, concentration) using sharp noses, prominent chins, and elongated, slanting eyes.
Found across major wall bands (jangha) to animate stone surfaces.
Religious Iconography
Anchored in Vaishnavite, Shaivite, and Jaina pantheons, reflecting complex Puranic theology.
Lakshmana Temple: Vaikuntha Vishnu in the garbhagriha.
Erotic Sculptures (Mithunas)

• Placed strategically on outer walls and junctions (sandhi-kshetra).
• Multiple interpretations include fertility symbolism, Tantric traditions, auspiciousness, worldly life preceding spiritual liberation, and cosmic union.
Kandariya Mahadeva: Intricate mithuna panels acting as transitional architectural anchors.
Narrative Panels and Storytelling
Displays a holistic worldview by juxtaposing sacred mythology with daily socio-political life (warriors, hunters, domestic scenes).
Lakshmana Temple Base: Continuous friezes depicting military processions, royal courts, and Ramayana episodes.
Attention to Ornamentation
Micro-carving of intricate drapery, heavy jewelry, girdles, and complex, stylized hairstyles.
Devi Jagadambi Temple: Highly adorned images of goddesses and celestial attendants.
Voluminous Tectonic Relief
Sculptures are organized in multiple horizontal tiers (jangha bands) and carved in high relief, nearly detaching from the back-wall.
Exterior walls of Kandariya Mahadeva, maximizing light and shadow play.

elements.text: Solanki Art and Architecture

The Solanki Dynasty (Chalukyas of Gujarat, 10th–13th century CE) developed a distinct regional style known as the Maru-Gurjara style, characterized by a synthesis of indigenous traditions and high technical precision. The Solanki sculptural tradition evolved from earlier regional styles, such as the 6th–8th century grey schist sculptures found at Samlaji, which mixed post-Gupta idioms with local traditions to create a distinct Gujarati aesthetic. This foundation eventually reached its maturity under Solanki patronage, influencing later Rajput and Western Indian art.
Distinctive Features of Solanki (Maru-Gurjara) Architecture

The Solanki style, also known as the Maru-Gurjara style (10th–13th century CE), is unique for its synthesis of high technical precision, scientific alignment, and the elevation of functional water structures into monumental art. The following reasons define its uniqueness compared to other Nagara or Dravida styles:

rows.text: "Inverted Temple" & Hydraulic Architecture
Unlike other Indian styles where water tanks are secondary, the Solanki style elevates functional water bodies into central, subterranean, elaborately carved "inverted temples."

• Rani-ki-vav (Patan): UNESCO stepwell acting as an underground sculptural museum.
• Surya Kund (Modhera): Stepped tank with 108 miniature shrines.
Solar Alignment
Exact east-west orientation in the Solanki temples allows equinox sunrays to traverse the assembly hall and illuminate the sanctum.
• Sun Temple (Modhera): Plain inner sanctum walls designed specifically for solar interaction.
Woodcarving Heritage in Stone
Transfers Gujarat’s rich woodcraft traditions to stone, yielding delicate "lace-like" deep undercutting.
• Dilwara Temples (Mt. Abu): Soft white marble ceiling medallions and bracket figures at Vimal Vasahi.
Autonomous Components
Unlike standard Nagara formats where halls are welded directly to the sanctum, the Solanki style separates the Sabha Mandapa into an independent, pillared island pavilion.
• Modhera Complex: The separate, stepped entrance leading from the Surya Kund directly up through the grand Torana into the open hall.
Interlocking Technique & Density
Constructed without binding mortar or lime, relying entirely on exquisite stone interlocking, tongue-and-groove jointing, and pure gravity physics.
• Taranga Jain Temple and the surviving ruins of the grand Rudramalaya Temple at Siddhpur.
Material Plurality
Diversifies beyond regional sandstone to utilize black basalt and soft marble.
• Early foundations at Samlaji (schist phase) evolving into the brilliant Mount Abu shrines (marble phase).

elements.text: 3. Rajput Paintings

Rajput painting evolved from earlier Western Indian manuscript traditions and matured under medieval Rajput courts. These schools evolved as a vibrant expression of regional identity, synthesizing indigenous folk traditions with the emotional depth of Bhakti philosophy, particularly through the revival of Shaivism and Vaishnavism.

rows.text: Bhakti & Regional Identity
Evolved as a visual language for the Bhakti Movement, transforming religious narratives into personal, emotional experiences rooted in local culture.
Gitagovinda Paintings: Celebrated the divine love of Radha and Krishna, reflecting the Vaishnavite revival.
Synthesis of Traditions

Represented a "brilliant synthesis" of indigenous Hindu traditions with Mughal realism. They adopted Mughal precision and naturalistic studies while retaining vibrant, symbolic two-dimensional perspectives.
Naturalistic Studies: Adopted Mughal-style delicate brushwork for depicting flora and fauna with high accuracy.
Decentralized Patronage
Flourished under the Samanta (feudal) system: Competitive regional centers, or Kalams, developed independently rather than following a single centralized imperial style.
Classification of Schools: Developed four distinct stylistic zones: Mewar, Marwar (Kishangarh/Jodhpur), Dhundhar (Amber/Jaipur), and Haroti (Bundi/Kota).
Dominant Themes
Focused on secular and religious cycles that linked human emotions to music, nature, and divinity.

• Ragamala: Depictions of musical modes.
• Baramasa: Illustrations of the twelve months and seasons.
Jain & Western Influence
Prolific financial and cultural support came from Jain merchant guilds (Shrenis). The early "Western Indian" style of the Solankis and Rashtrakutas provided the template for later Rajput miniatures.
Illustrated Manuscripts: Early Jaina texts funded by merchants preceded and influenced Rajput court art.

elements.text: Comparison: Rajput vs. Mughal Paintings

rows.text: Core Theme
Primarily Devotional (Bhakti, Krishna-Lila) and Mythological
Primarily Secular and Aristocratic (Court durbars, battles, royal hunts, imperial portraits).
Patronage
Decentralized; multiple regional feudal courts (Samantas)
Centralized imperial workshop (Tasvir Khana) controlled by the Emperor
Philosophy
Emotional, symbolic, and rooted in community/ folk traditions
Realistic, detailed, and used for imperial propaganda
Color Usage
Bold, vibrant primary colors (reds, yellows, indigos)
Muted, refined palettes with a focus on shading and 3D depth
Perspective
Often two-dimensional or conceptual
Strongly influenced by European perspective and realism
Notable Examples

1. The Bani Thani painting (Kishangarh School by Nihal Chand), often called the "Radha of Rajasthan."
2. Ragamala Series: Visual depictions of Indian musical modes like Raga Megha

1. Hamzanama: Manuscript depicting the adventures of Amir Hamza (during Akbar)
2. Ustad Mansur's highly accurate scientific studies of flora/fauna under Jahangir.

elements.text: 4. Decline of the Rajput Dynasties

The decline of the Rajput Dynasties (8th–12th century CE) was not the result of a single event but a combination of internal structural weaknesses, persistent infighting, and the military superiority of invading Turkic forces.

rows.text: Internal Structural & Political Weaknesses

• Decentralized Feudalism: Over-reliance on clan vassals (Samantas) instead of a centralized standing army delayed strategic mobilization.
• Persistent Infighting: Intense inter-clan rivalries prevented a pan-Indian collective security front.
• Mutual Exhaustion: Long-term fallout of the early medieval Tripartite Struggle left the regional states fragmented and economically depleted.
Military and Tactical Deficiencies

• Cavalry Inferiority: Heavy reliance on slow, unpredictable war elephants against the highly fluid Turkish forces.
• Tactical Inflexibility: Strict adherence to codes of chivalry over strategic realism.
• Turkic Innovations: Superior mobility using Central Asian steeds, horse archers, and deceptive tactics (e.g., feigned retreats).
Decisive External Invasions

• Ghaznavid Economic Drain: Systemic raids plundered institutional wealth, crippling regional financial stability. ♦Example: Mahmud of Ghazni: Sacked Somnath Temple (reign of Bhima I).
• Ghurid Consolidation: Decisive battlefield victories systematically dismantled North Indian Hindu principalities. ♦Example: Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE): Paved the way for the Delhi Sultanate.
• Sultanate Expansion: Aggressive siege warfare broke down formidable strategic strongholds. ♦Example: Alauddin Khilji: Successfully besieged Chittor and Ranthambore.
The Mughal Era and Integration

• Strategic Subservience: Shift from absolute sovereignty to negotiated regional autonomy under a paramount power. ♦Example: Mewar (Sisodiyas): Stiff resistance under Rana Pratap, contrasting with the diplomatic capitulation of other clans.
• Administrative Absorption: Integration into the Mansabdari system, which converted independent rulers into imperial military commanders. ♦Example: Amber (Kachhwahas) & Marwar (Rathores): Accepted Mughal suzerainty.

elements.text: The Rajput period reshaped India's political and cultural landscape through regional state formation, temple architecture, martial traditions, and enduring contributions to art, literature, and local governance.
Kakatiya Dynasty (12th - 14th century)

The Kakatiya Dynasty, a Telugu dynasty, ruled much of the eastern Deccan region (present-day Telangana and Andhra Pradesh) between the 12th and 14th centuries, with Warangal as their capital. The recent discovery of a 13th-century inscription underscores the enduring historical significance of the Kakatiya Dynasty and offers further insights into their reign, particularly that of Rudrama Devi.
Art and Architecture under the Kakatiyas
The Kakatiya Dynasty (12th–14th century CE) significantly enriched South Indian temple architecture by blending regional traditions with advanced engineering and artistic finesse.
Key Architectural Features
• Trikuta Style (Triple Shrine): A signature plan involving three sanctums—usually dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu, and
Surya—connected to a common mandapa.

♦Example: The Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda.
• Stellate (Star-shaped) Platforms: Temples were built on raised, star-shaped platforms called Jagati, which provided both

structural stability and a dynamic aesthetic through light and shadow play.
• Lathe-Turned Pillars: The use of black granite for pillars, polished to a high mirror-like finish using lathe-turning

techniques and adorned with intricate floral and geometric patterns.
• Keerthi Toranas: Monumental, freestanding arched gateways that are unique to the Kakatiya style and served as grand
entrances to fort and temple complexes.
Sculptural Art
Kakatiya sculptures are noted for their realism and cultural detail:
• Secular Themes: Intricate carvings depicting warriors, optical illusions, and even contemporary fashion like elaborate

costumes, ornaments, footwear, warriors and everyday life.
• Perini Shivatandavam: The sculpture panels often captured the warrior dance form that flourished under royal patronage.
Contribution to South Indian Architecture
The Kakatiyas introduced pioneering engineering techniques that made their temples more durable and lighter:
• Sandbox Technology: Sandbox foundation technology improved structural stability by using layers of sand, lime, charcoal,

and other materials beneath the foundation, enhancing load distribution and resistance to ground movement. Lightweight porous bricks with low density used in the vimana to reduce dead load.
• Floating Bricks: They engineered lightweight, porous bricks for temple towers to reduce the total weight on the foundation.

♦Example: The Ramappa Temple (a UNESCO World Heritage site).
• Hydraulic Integration: Temples were often built in proximity to massive man-made irrigation tanks (lakes) like the Pakala
and Ramappa Lakes, making the temple a hub for agrarian redistribution and water management.
Synthesis of Nagara and Dravida Elements in Kakatiya Architecture
The Kakatiya dynasty masterfully fused Northern and Southern architectural practices. A few examples are as follows:
• Ramappa Temple (Palampet): Dravidian stepped shikhara uniquely constructed with engineered lightweight floating

bricks over a Vesara-inspired stellate plan supporting a predominantly Dravidian superstructure.
• Warangal Fort: Monumental freestanding gateways unique to Kakatiya architecture, possibly inspired by earlier Buddhist
torana traditions.

rows.text:
• Curvilinear Shikharas: Many temples feature graceful, curving shikharas topped with an amalaka (ribbed stone disc) and a kalasa finial, hallmark traits of North Indian temple design.
• Bhumija Elements: Borrowing from the Central Indian Bhumija style, architects utilized miniature decorative spires and rhythmic, grid-like geometric patterns on the tower walls.

• Pyramidal Vimana: The towering sanctum roofs were designed in the traditional squarish, stepped-pyramidal Vimana style.
• Mandapa Layout: The inclusion of pillared assembly halls (Sabha Mandapa and Ranga Mandapa) in front of the sanctum directly reflects South Indian temple planning.
• Gateway Design: The famed Kala Thoranam arches (found at the Warangal Fort) feature ornamental pillars and decorative elements that evolved from Dravidian gopuram traditions.

elements.text: The Kakatiya dynasty transformed the Deccan through decentralized governance, tank-based irrigation, Telugu cultural renaissance, and fortified urban centres, leaving a lasting imprint on South India's socio-economic landscape.
Foreign Invasions in India

The mediaeval period in India (8th–16th century CE) was marked by a series of foreign incursions that permanently altered the subcontinent’s political, cultural, and economic landscape. These invasions, primarily from West and Central Asia, introduced Islamic institutions and led to the evolution of a unique composite culture.
Causes of Foreign Invasions
• Vast Wealth: India's fabulous wealth, particularly stored in major temple centers, acted as a primary magnet for invaders

seeking to replenish their treasuries.
• Political Fragmentation: The collapse of strong central authorities (like the post-Harsha vacuum) and the exhaustion

caused by internal conflicts like the Tripartite Struggle left India vulnerable.
• Military Technology Gap: Indian rulers relied heavily on slow war elephants, which were easily outmanoeuvred by the

highly mobile, professional Turkish cavalry and mounted archers.
• Expansionist Ambitions: Invaders sought to establish garrison towns and control trade routes to ensure a regular flow of

tribute and plunder.
• Internal Divisions & Alliances: Disunity and internal conflicts sometimes led local rulers to invite or assist foreign

invaders against their internal rivals. For example, prior to the pivotal First Battle of Panipat (1526), discontented Afghan chieftains and local nobles actively invited Babur to invade and overthrow the ruling Lodi Empire.
Consequences of Foreign Invasions
• Establishment of Muslim Rule: Invasions led to the foundation of the Delhi Sultanate and later the Mughal Empire,

shifting the power center to Delhi.
• Indo-Islamic Synthesis: A "cultural mosaic" emerged, blending Persian and Indian styles in architecture (arch/dome),

music (Rabab/Sarangi), and literature.
• Economic Impact: While raids caused an immediate economic drain, the establishment of the Sultanate revived internal

trade, reintroduced standardised coinage, monetised the economy, and expanded long-distance trade.
• Military Reforms: Constant threats, especially from Mongols, pressured Indian rulers to adopt permanent standing

armies and advanced fortifications like Siri Fort.
• Social & Religious Changes: Deepened social stratification and led to the rise of syncretic spiritual traditions like the

Bhakti and Sufi movements.
• Technological Advancement: Introduced new industrial expertise such as paper-making and the spinning wheel, which
significantly increased textile production.
Indo-Islamic Synthesis

In the medieval period (8th–18th century CE), foreign rulers—primarily of Turkic, Afghan, Persian, and Mongol origin—did not remain external entities but engaged in a profound Indo-Islamic synthesis instead of remaining external influences. This process transformed India into a "cultural mosaic," where foreign institutions merged with local traditions to create unique composite forms of governance, art, and social life.
Domain Description Examples

rows.text: Architectural Synthesis

• Structural Fusion: Blended foreign structural engineering (true arch, dome, voussoir technique) with indigenous decorative motifs.
• Regional Adaptation: Absorbed local vernacular architectural styles into imperial Islamic monuments.

• Alai Darwaza: first mature true dome built by Alauddin Khilji (1311 CE)
• Bangla Roof: Adoption of the curved bamboo-roof style of Bengal huts into Sultanate and Mughal buildings.
Governance & Social Integration

• Administrative Inclusion: Maintained a distinct religious identity but deeply integrated local elites into the state apparatus.
• Political Legitimacy: Adopted indigenous cultural symbols to foster local acceptance and governance stability.

• Akbar’s Mansabdari System: Institutionalized high-ranking inclusion of Rajputs and Hindus.
• Ghurid Coinage: Mu'izzuddin Ghori struck gold coins featuring the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
Linguistic & Literary Fusion

• Vernacular Evolution: Interaction of Persian (court language) with local dialects created hybrid idioms.
• The Translation Movement: State-sponsored translation of Sanskrit classics to foster administrative and cultural bridge-building.

• Development of Urdu: A linguistic blend of Persian, Arabic, and regional dialects.
• Razmnama: The Mahabharata translated into Persian under Akbar.
• Dara Shukoh: Translated the Upanishads into Persian.
Artistic & Spiritual Syncretism

• Musical & Dance Evolution: Combined Persian/ Central Asian structural styles with classical Indian modes.
• Mughal Miniature Painting: A synthesis of Persian realism, landscape depth, and indigenous Indian colors/themes.
• Spiritual Confluence: Parallel growth of mysticism that preached universal brotherhood and egalitarianism.

• Amir Khusrau: Introduced the Sitar and Tabla; developed the Qawwali musical form.
• Kathak: Transformed into a major classical form through Mughal court patronage.
• Sufi & Bhakti Movements: Shared spiritual ground concepts like Wahdat-al-Wujud (Unity of Being/Monism) and Nirguna Upasana (devotion to a formless divine entity).

elements.text: While invasions caused disruption and destruction, they also enriched India’s cultural mosaic through Indo-Persian art, architecture, and ideas, laying the foundations for medieval syncretism.
Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE)

The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) was established by rulers of Turkish and Afghan origin. It introduced Persian culture, administrative reforms, and significant advancements in architecture, literature, and technology.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. What were the major technological changes introduced during the Sultanate period? How did those technological changes influence Indian society? (2023)
1. The Advent of Delhi Sultanate
The arrival of the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century marked a transition from a fragmented landscape of regional warrior clans to a centralized Indo-Islamic state.
Conditions Prevalent in India at the Advent of the Delhi Sultanate

North India was politically fragmented, with multiple regional kingdoms and ongoing rivalries, hollowed out by decentralized feudalism, bitter inter-clan rivalries, and devastating economic plundering.

• Political Fragmentation: By the 10th century, major powers like the Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas had collapsed. North India splintered into smaller autonomous dynasties including the Tomaras (Delhi), Chauhans (Rajasthan), Solankis (Gujarat), and Chandelas (Bundelkhand).
• Decentralized Feudalism: Governance relied on the Samanta system, where rulers depended on local vassal chiefs for troops rather than maintaining large standing armies.

• Lack of Unity: Constant territorial disputes and rivalries among these regional rulers (like Prithviraj Chauhan and Jayachandra) prevented them from forming a united front against external invasions.
• Economic Drain: Systemic raids by earlier invaders like Mahmud of Ghazni (17 raids between 1000–1027 CE) plundered wealthy temple centers, crippling regional financial stability.
The Rise of the Delhi Sultanate
The collapse of the Gurjara-Pratiharas and the exhaustion from the Tripartite Struggle left North India politically fragmented. This power vacuum created favourable conditions for Turkish expansion.
• Military Superiority:
 Mobility: The Turkish cavalry was far superior to the Rajput forces, which relied on slow-moving war elephants.
 Tactics: Turks utilized mounted archers and brilliant cavalry maneuvers, while Rajputs often adhered to rigid traditional codes of chivalry (Dharmayuddha).
• The Bandagan System: The Sultanate utilized specialized military slaves who were bought, trained in governance and warfare, and paid in cash, ensuring high loyalty and discipline.
• Centralized Authority: Unlike the decentralized Rajput clans, the early Sultans established a monolithic state with strategic Iqta land grants to maintain administrative control.
• Tactical Realism: Turkic armies relied on highly mobile cavalry and skilled horse archers, which easily outmanoeuvred the slower Rajput infantry and war elephants.
• The Mamluk Institution: The use of highly trained, fiercely loyal military slave officers (Mamluks) created a merit-based command structure less prone to regional tribal biases.
• Economic Consolidation: Drastic market regulations, price controls, and systematic agricultural taxation (like the Kharaj) successfully funded continuous territorial expansion.

The rise of the Delhi Sultanate was a triumph of centralized, professional statecraft over decentralized feudalism. By replacing regional warrior traditions with a disciplined imperial bureaucracy, it set the stage for a four-century-long Indo-Islamic political synthesis.
2. Socio-economic Conditions in the Delhi Sultanate
The Socio-Economic conditions during the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE) were defined by the introduction of new administrative institutions, technological shifts, and a profound cultural synthesis.
ECONOMIC CONDITIONS

rows.text: Agrarian Economy & Revenue

• Cash-based Revenue: Increasing monetization encouraged payment of revenue in cash in several regions, promoting commercialization and urban growth.
• Iqta System: Institutionalized by Iltutmish; land grants (Iqtas) given to officials (muqtis) to maintain royal troops.
• Fiscal/Market Reforms: Alauddin Khalji fixed revenue (Kharaj) at 50% and instituted strict price controls to sustain a massive standing army.
• State Agrarian Interventions: Muhammad bin Tughlaq created Diwan-i-Amir Kohi (Dept. of Agriculture) for farmer credit; Firuz Shah Tughlaq built extensive irrigation canals.
Trade & Urbanization

• Urban Revival: Rapid expansion of domestic and external trade (via Central Asia and oceanic routes); growth of urban cities like Delhi.
• Merchant Networks: Traditional guilds lost much of their earlier prominence, while merchant communities increasingly organized through caste and regional networks.
Monetization

• Currency Standardization: Introduction of the silver tanka and copper jital by Iltutmish.
• Monetary Crisis: M.B. Tughlaq’s token bronze/copper currency experiment failed disastrously due to mass forgery.
Technology & Industry

• Manufacturing Shifts: Introduction of the spinning wheel (charkha) boosted yarn output substantially; sericulture (silk) expanded significantly in Bengal; paper-making introduced.
• Construction: Revolutionized by brick, lime mortar, and advanced vaulting techniques.

elements.text: SOCIAL CONDITIONS

rows.text: Social Stratification

• Ruling Elite Hierarchy: Monopolized initially by Central Asian Turks; Afghans and Indian Muslims integrated later.
• The Chahalgani ("The Forty"): Elite corps of military slaves (Bandagan) who dominated early politics until Balban crushed them to centralize power.
• Institutional Slavery: Slaves acted as domestics, artisans, and commanders. Firuz Tughlaq maintained thousands of slaves, systematically training them in handicrafts.
Status of Women

• Upper-class women: They faced seclusion (purdah/zenana) but retained legal rights to property inheritance and divorce.
• Political Exception: Raziya Sultana broke barriers to rule directly, commanding forces in male attire.
Cultural Synthesis

• Religious Dynamics: Coexistence of Hinduism and Islam; Sufi and Bhakti traditions promoted devotional spirituality and facilitated cultural interaction, although communal and political conflicts also persisted.
• Language & Education: Early Hindavi evolved through interaction between Persian and local dialects, eventually contributing to Urdu; state-funded Maktabs and Madrasas institutionalized education.

elements.text: Role of the Iqta System in the Delhi Sultanate

The Iqta system served as the administrative and military backbone of the Delhi Sultanate, primarily institutionalised by Sultan Iltutmish. It was a mechanism for assigning revenue-yielding land parcels to nobles and officers in lieu of cash salaries, ensuring the state could maintain a professional military and local governance without a massive central bureaucracy.

rows.text: Military Support
Decentralized funding of the army; Iqtadars (or Muqtis) used local revenue to maintain troops for royal service.
This provided a ready force for military campaigns without draining the central treasury.
Fiscal Control
Iqtadars managed provincial taxation and were required to remit the surplus revenue (fawasil) to the central treasury.
Established a clear chain of command between the capital and the province.
Transferable Nature
To prevent regional power centers, iqtas were transferable and rotated every few years to stop officials from establishing hereditary roots.
Balban utilized this to keep his "Forty" Turkish nobles in check.
Territorial Expansion
Ambitious commanders were granted large iqtas on turbulent frontiers as an incentive to conquer and pacify new lands.
This strategy facilitated the rapid consolidation of North India under the early Mamluk rulers.
Economic & Urban Growth
The presence of military garrisons required local craftsmen and traders, promoting regional trade and the growth of markets.
Led to a new phase of urban growth as rural products were drawn into towns to pay taxes in cash.
Limitations of the Iqta System
Distance and weak central authority often led to rebellions; distant provinces like Bengal and Sind were the first to break free.
Reintroduction of hereditary iqtas under Firuz Shah Tughlaq weakened central control and led to noble intrigues.

elements.text: Market Reforms of Alauddin Khalji

Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) implemented a radical set of market reforms primarily to sustain a massive permanent standing army on a limited treasury. By legally fixing prices and suppressing inflation, he ensured that his soldiers, who were paid in cash, could afford essential commodities without the state's finances being drained.
The Sultan introduced several short-term, high-impact reforms:
• Price Standardization: Legally fixed prices for all essential goods, from grains to livestock.
• Market Specialization: Created three distinct markets: Mandi (grains), Sarai Adl (cloth/merchandise), and a market for horses/slaves.
• Administrative Oversight: Established the Diwan-i-Riyasat and appointed a Shahna-i-Mandi (superintendent) to regulate trade.
• Surveillance: Deployed a secret intelligence network of Barids and Munhiyans to report on market activities.
• Resource Management: Built government storehouses to prevent hoarding and ensure rationing during famines.
Features and Impact of Market Reforms

rows.text: Military & Strategic
Fixed low rates for horses, armor, and provisions allowed for a permanent standing army.
Military Supremacy: The Sultanate successfully repelled repeated Mongol invasions.
Economic Control
Strictly monitored the buying, selling, and bargaining in the bazaars via daily reports.
Stability: Arrested inflation and maintained a stable urban populace in Delhi.
Regulatory Rigor
Severe punishments for weight deficiency, such as cutting equal weight of flesh from the seller.
Resentment: The draconian nature of the laws left traders oppressed and fostered rampant corruption among officials.
Rural Impact
Collected land taxes directly from cultivators and fixed revenue at 50% of produce.
Hardship for Producers: Farmers were forced to sell grain at state-dictated rates, regardless of their own production costs.
Governance & Sustainability
Relied on a centralized, coercive bureaucratic machinery rather than natural economic dynamics.
Short-Lived Legacy: The system collapsed almost immediately after Alauddin's death as it depended on his "iron will".

elements.text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Visionary But Controversial Ruler

Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign (1325–1351) was a period of profound transition and ambitious experimentation within the Delhi Sultanate. He is characterised not as a "mad king," but as a deeply learned, idealistic visionary whose innovative structural ideas collapsed due to severe administrative overreach, rigid implementation, and a lack of consistent bureaucratic support.

headers: The Visionary Statecraft: Rationality Behind the Experiments
The Crisis of Execution: Why the Policies Collapsed

rows.text:
• Geopolitical Realities & Centralized Governance: He transferred the capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri) because its central location and impregnable fort provided a strategic base to rule South India and the Deccan more effectively, & Delhi was too close to the vulnerable northwest Mongol invasion corridor.
• Fiscal Innovation Amid Bullion Crisis: A global silver shortage coupled with empty state reserves after expansive military mobilization prompted the creation of a fiduciary currency system.
• Agrarian Modernization & Institutionalization: He established the Diwan-i-Amir Kohi (Department of Agriculture) and provided state credit (Sondhar/Takkavi) to peasants to expand cultivation and maximize revenue.

• Rigid Implementation & Lack of Pragmatism: Rather than a gradual administrative shift, he ordered a forced, total evacuation of Delhi's elite populace to Daulatabad, causing immense suffering.
• Institutional Deficit & Lack of Oversight: The state failed to maintain a monopoly on minting, leading to widespread forgery of bronze coins, which forced the Sultan to exchange them for genuine silver, draining the treasury. (As Barani noted, "the house of every Hindu turned into a domestic mint.")
• Ecological and Strategic Miscalculations: He launched heavy tax hikes (50% of produce) in the Doab during a severe, active famine, leading to arbitrary and oppressive revenue collection that sparked uprisings.

elements.text: Impacts: Sociopolitical Backlash & Imperial Fragmentation
• Alienation of the Nobility and Ulema: His secular outlook and his merciless punishments for those who could not

execute his rapid changes alienated his support base.
• Peasant Resistance and Agrarian Crisis: Widespread agrarian rebellions in the fertile Doab region led to a severe

contraction of the empire's primary revenue base.
• Centralizing Tendencies and Decline: These failures triggered independence movements, directly leading to the birth of

the Vijayanagara (1336) and Bahmani (1347) Empires, and rebellions in Bengal and Madurai. Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s failure was not a failure of intellect, but of execution and timing. Modern historians evaluate him as an intellectual ruler "ahead of his time" whose administrative frameworks, such as agricultural credit, laid foundational stepping stones for future reforms.
3. Art and Architecture in the Delhi Sultanate
Evolution of Sultanate Architecture

The architecture of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE) represents the emergence and refinement of the Indo-Islamic (or Indo-Saracenic) style, a synthesis of West Asian structural engineering with indigenous Indian decorative traditions.
New Features of the Delhi Sultanate Architecture:
• Arcuate Form: The Sultanate introduced the true arch and dome, replacing the traditional Indian trabeated (post-and-lintel) system.
• Engineering Tools: Utilized squinches and pendentives to transition square walls into round bases, allowing domes to span massive spaces without interior pillars.
• Materials: Structures primarily used rubble masonry cased with chunam (limestone plaster) or dressed stones like red sandstone and white marble.
• Ornamentation & Calligraphy: Avoided living forms; focused instead on arabesque (intertwined floral lines), geometric grids, and Quranic calligraphy (Kufic, Naskh styles).
• Syncretic Motifs: Traditional Indian elements such as lotus motifs, brackets, and bell-and-chain patterns were frequently integrated into monuments.
• Use of Spolia: Converted pre-existing Hindu and Jain temple materials into early Islamic structures (e.g., columned corridors in early mosques).

• Mausoleums & Forts: Simple graves evolved into monumental tomb architecture (shifting from square bases to advanced octagonal layouts). Fortified cities featured thick, sloping outer walls (batter) for structural durability and defense.
• Regional Adaptation:
 Bengal: Adopted local curved bamboo roof styles, leading to the "Bangla roof" used in Sultanate and later Mughal buildings.
 Gujarat: Borrowed heavily from regional temple traditions, incorporating toranas and carved tree panels into mosques and dargahs.
Chronological Evolution:

rows.text: Mamluk (Slave) (1206–1290)
Initially focused on converting existing structures. Characterized by the birth of the Qutb complex and the introduction of the first true arch.
Qutub Minar (243-ft tapering tower); Tomb of Balban (first true arch).
Marked by a shift toward technical precision. Introduced an austere style known as Khalji Style.
Alai Darwaza: First example of scientific use of true arch and dome in Sultanate architecture Siri Fort: The first new medieval city built with thick rubble defensive walls to counter Mongol raids.
Developed a robust, austere style using sloping (batter) walls to increase structural stability. Focused on massive fortifications and public works.
Tughlaqabad Fort; Tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq; Indo-Islamic architecture with battering walls, a marble dome, and three graves
Sayyid & Lodi (1414–1526)
Introduced octagonal tomb plans and double domes, marking a transition that heavily influenced later Mughal aesthetics.
Tomb of Sikandar Lodi; Tomb of Muhammad Shah

elements.text: 4. Arts

rows.text: Persian and Central Asian Influence
Sultanate rulers invited Persian artists → Influence of Persian, Turkish, and Central Asian styles
Persian miniature painting style influenced later Mughal paintings
Islamic Calligraphy
Arabic and Persian calligraphy (Kufic, Naskh) were used for decoration.
Quranic verses in Kufic script inscribed on the Qutb Minar.
Geometric and Floral Designs
Intricate geometric patterns and floral motifs instead of human representations.
Floral arabesque designs in the Alai Darwaza.
Metalwork and Coin Art
Synthesis of indigenous Indian craftsmanship and Islamic artistic influences from Persia and Central Asia.
Coins of Alauddin Khalji bore stylized inscriptions; Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued token currency with artistic calligraphy.
Textile and Carpet Weaving
Promoted fine textiles, introducing new weaving techniques
Silk brocades from Gujarat; carpet weaving inspired by Persian styles.
Glazed Pottery
Glazed pottery flourished with colorful designs used in decoration.
Blue-glazed pottery from Hauz Khas excavations.

elements.text: 5. Literature

rows.text: Persian as the Court Language
Persian became the dominant language of administration, literature, and poetry

• Tabaqat-i-Nasiri by Minhaj-i-Siraj
• Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Ziauddin Barani
Royal Patronage
Sultans encouraged poets, historians, and scholars to write on administration, history, and religion.

• Alauddin Khalji patronized Amir Khusrau.
• Firoz Shah Tughlaq supported historian Ziauddin Barani.
Amir Khusrau’s Contributions
Known as the “Parrot of India,” wrote in Persian and Hindavi, shaping early Hindustani literature.

• Historical: Qiran-us-Sa'dain
• Sufi and devotional poetry: Qawwali
• Music: Ghazals and Tarana, etc.
Historical Writing Flourished
Political and social history in Persian chronicles → valuable insights into governance, wars, and administration.

• Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi by Ziauddin Barani → history of Tughlaq dynasty.
• Futuh-us-Salatin by Abdul Malik Isami → early Islamic conquests in India.
Vernacular Literature
Regional languages such as Hindi, Punjabi, and Bengali gained literary importance
• Baba Farid (Punjabi Sufi literature)
Religious and Sufi Literature
Sufi saints wrote extensively on mysticism, spirituality, and devotion, blending Persian, Arabic, and local languages.

• Fawaid-ul-Fuad by Amir Hasan Sijzi
• Miftah-ul-Fuqarah by Hamiduddin Nagauri
Translations and Commentaries
Islamic texts (Quran and Hadiths) and Hindu texts, were translated into Persian and accompanied by commentaries.
• Firoz Shah Tughlaq patronized translations of Sanskrit astronomical texts.

elements.text: 6. Technological Innovations and Their Impact on Indian Society

The arrival and establishment of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526 CE) introduced several transformative technological innovations from West and Central Asia. These changes significantly impacted India's economy, architecture, and social organization, contributing to the evolution of a unique "cultural mosaic".

rows.text: Textile Production
Introduction of the spinning wheel (Charkha) most likely from Iran in the 14th century and the use of treadles in looms.
Increased yarn production, revolutionizing the textile industry and enabling a massive expansion in fabric output.
Paper-making Technology
A Chinese invention introduced in India during the rule of the Sultans.
Transformed administration, record-keeping, and literature, fostering a strong school of historical writing (e.g., Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi).
Persian Wheel (Rahat)
The integration of a right-angled pin-gearing system to the old Ghati-Yantra, driven by animal power.
Boosted agricultural productivity and stabilized the urban food supply by allowing more efficient water distribution to fields.
Architectural Construction
Introduction of the voussoir technique (interlocking blocks) for true arches and domes, alongside lime mortar and vaulting.
Enabled the spanning of vast internal spaces without pillars. Examples include the Alai Darwaza and Balban’s Tomb.
Sericulture (Silk Production)
The science of rearing silkworms expanded significantly in Bengal by the 15th century.
Enriched the commercial economy by introducing high-value silk products for both domestic luxury use and international trade.
Astrolabes
Persian astronomical instruments used for navigation and timekeeping.
Enhanced precision in timekeeping for administrative schedules and religious prayers, while laying the groundwork for future astronomical studies.

elements.text: The Delhi Sultanate transformed India's political landscape through administrative centralization, military innovations, urbanization, and Indo-Islamic cultural synthesis, laying enduring foundations for the Mughal Empire.
Hoysala Dynasty (10th-14th century)

Hoysala Dynasty ruled over parts of modern-day Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu. Initially, feudatories of the Western Chalukyas, they rose to prominence and left an indelible mark on South Indian history through their contributions to art, architecture, literature, and governance. Their capitals, Halebidu and Belur, became centres of cultural and political activity during their golden age.
1. Economic Organisation and Social Structure

rows.text: Agriculture
Mainstay of economy; irrigation through tanks & canals
State-Sponsored Tanks: Shantisagara, Vishnusagara, and Ballalarayasagara
Revenue System
Land revenue primary; taxes on trade, markets, professionals

• Land Revenue: Siddhaya
• Cattle tax: Bala-vana
• Loom tax: Magga-dere
• Other Revenues: dere, vana, nimandi, tanda, dandya, etc.
Artisanal Production
Guilds (Shrenis) for weavers, blacksmiths, sculptors, goldsmiths
Belur-Halebidu sculptural workshops; weaving centres in Karnataka
Caste System
Varna-based but flexible in practice; Shudras & women engaged in economic activity
Guilds open to multiple communities
Religious Pluralism
Vaishnavism, Shaivism, and Jainism flourished under royal patronage
Vishnuvardhana (Vaishnavite); Ballala II (Shaiva); Jain temples at Shravanabelagola

elements.text: 2. Art

rows.text: Sculpture

• Intricate, miniature-like detailing
• Soapstone (Chloritic Schist) allowed precision
• Panels depict mythological, social, musical, erotic, and martial scenes
• Madanikas (celestial damsels) at Chennakeshava Temple, Belur
Multi-tiered Friezes
• Horizontal friezes depicting animals, mythological scenes, and floral designs.
• Friezes of Mahabharata and Ramayana at Halebidu
Iconography

• Emphasis on deities with multi-limbed dynamism
• Themes from Bhagavata, Shaiva, Jain, and local myths

• Vishnu as Chennakeshava (handsome Vishnu) at Belur
• Shiva as Ardhanarishvara, Gajasurasamhara in Halebidu
Performing Arts

• Dance and music central to temple rituals
• Patronage to classical and folk forms

• Queen Shantala Devi: skilled dancer and patron
• Nritya Ganika figures on pillars

elements.text: Temple Architecture

The Hoysala Dynasty (c. 10th–14th century CE) developed a unique architectural idiom in the Southern Deccan (modern Karnataka). Originally feudatories of the Western Chalukyas, they refined the Vesara (hybrid) style to its ultimate decorative limit, characterized by star-shaped plans and miniature-like stone carvings.
Key Characteristics of Hoysala Architecture

rows.text: Stellate (Star-shaped) Plan
The ground plan consists of multiple projecting angles, transforming a square layout into a complex star shape.
Chennakesava Temple, Belur.
Soapstone Medium
Use of Chloritic Schist (Soapstone), which is soft when quarried, allowed artists to execute extremely intricate, jewelry-like carvings.
Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebid.
Lathe-turned Pillars
Highly polished, symmetrical, cylindrical pillars that appear as if they were turned on a wood lathe.
Parsvanatha Basadi, Halebid.
Multi-tiered Friezes
Horizontal bands at the temple base featuring a continuous procession of elephants, lions, and scenes from epics.
Ramayana and Mahabharata friezes at Halebid.
Trikuta (Triple Shrine)
A structural layout featuring three sanctums dedicated to different deities, connected to a common central hall.
Keshava Temple, Somanathapura.
Raised Platform (Jagati)
The entire temple complex is built on a wide, star-shaped raised platform used for circumambulation.
Belur and Halebid temples.
Madanikas
Exquisite bracket figures of celestial dancers (Madanikas or Salabhanjikas) shown in dynamic rhythmic poses.
Chennakesava Temple, Belur.

elements.text: Distinctiveness from Nagara and Dravida Schools

The Hoysala style of architecture is considered distinct from the Nagara (Northern) and Dravida (Southern) schools because it represents an independent, highly ornate hybrid style known as the Vesara (or Deccan) idiom, characterized by star-shaped ground plans and intricate, soapstone-carved surface decorations.

rows.text: Ground Plan
Primarily square with projections.
Often rectangular with concentric walls.
Unique Stellate (star-shaped) plan.
Tower (Spire)
Curvilinear Shikhara rising to a point.
Stepped pyramidal Vimana.
Hybrid stepped-pyramidal towers that are often shorter and more ornate.
Decorative Density
Focus on vertical thrust; balanced ornamentation.
Monumental scale with grand gopurams.
Extreme horror vacui; every inch of the surface is covered in minute, intricate detail.
Material
Usually Sandstone or Granite.
Primarily hard Granite.
Soapstone (Schist) for micro-level detail.

elements.text: The Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebid, and Somanathapura are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites, recognized as the "Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas"
3. Literature

rows.text: Kannada and Sanskrit Patronage
Encouraged both Kannada and Sanskrit literature; Kannada literary production expanded significantly.
Sanskrit scholar Trivikramapandita.
Development of Kannada Metres
The Shatpadi (six-line), Tripadi (three-line), and Ragale (a highly musical, rhymed narrative poetic metre) became popular.
Raghavanka’s Harishchandra Kavya popularized Shatpadi metre.
Religious and Philosophical Texts
Jain, Shaiva, and Vaishnava texts were written. Dvaita philosophy was also developed.
Madhvacharya authored the Brahma Sutra Bhashya, Rig Bhashya
Jain and Shaiva Epics
Jain and Shaiva authors wrote Kannada versions of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.
Nagachandra’s Ramachandra Charitapurana (Jain Ramayana).
Vachana and Bhakti Literature
Virashaiva saints wrote Vachanas (prose poems) in simple Kannada.
Basavanna's Vachanas; Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi's devotional poetry.
Historical and Biographical Works
Many works glorified kings and saints.
Rudrabhatta’s Jagannatha Vijaya (about Krishna).
Scientific and Secular Texts
Literature included grammar, medicine, mathematics, and rhetoric.
Kesiraja’s Shabdamanidarpana (Grammar).

elements.text: The Hoysala dynasty's legacy endures through its magnificent temples at Belur, Halebid, and Somanathapur, now UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Renowned for intricate architecture, these "Sacred Ensembles" mark India's 42nd UNESCO listing, celebrating the dynasty's artistic and cultural brilliance. The Hoysala legacy contributed to the later Vijayanagara temple design philosophy, continuing their stylistic features.
Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE)

The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) was founded by Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama dynasty on the southern banks of the Tungabhadra River. It emerged in the aftermath of the decline of the Hoysalas, Kakatiyas, and Kampili kingdom and became the principal political power resisting the expansion of the Delhi Sultanate in South India.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Krishnadeva Raya, the king of Vijayanagar, was not only an accomplished scholar himself but was also a great patron of learning and literature. Discuss. (2016)

rows.text:
• Harihara I & Bukka I: According to tradition, Harihara and Bukka established the empire under the spiritual guidance of Vidyaranya of Sringeri Math.
• Harihara II: Expanded towards Goa, Belgaum and Konkan through prolonged conflicts with Bahmani rulers.
• Deva Raya I: Built Tungabhadra dam; hired Turkic archers; visited by Nicolo Conti.
• Deva Raya II: Greatest Sangama king; titled Gajabetegara (Elephant Hunter).

• Saluva Narasimha: Saved empire from collapse via First Usurpation.
• Immadi Narasimha: Reigned during Vasco da Gama’s arrival at Calicut (1498).

• Krishna Deva Raya: Territorial & cultural zenith; titled Abhinava Bhoja; captured Raichur Doab; wrote Amuktamalyada; patronized Ashtadiggajas.
• Achyuta Deva Raya: Patronized Purandaradasa; visited by Fernao Nuniz.
• Sada Siva Raya: Puppet ruler; regent Rama Raya lost Battle of Talaikotta (1565).

• Tirumala: Shifted capital to Penukonda after Hampi's destruction.
• Venkata II: Shifted capital to Chandragiri; saw emergence of Mysore (Wodeyars).
• Sri Ranga III: The final independent monarch before complete fragmentation.

elements.text: 1. Political Structure and Administration

rows.text: Centralized Monarchy
King as supreme authority; hereditary succession; symbol of divine rule (such as Virupaksha).
Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529 CE) titled "Hindu-rāya-suratrāṇa" (Sultan among Hindu kings).
Administrative Units
Empire was divided into Rajyas (provinces), Nadus (districts), Sthalas (sub-districts), Gramas (villages).
Hoysala Rajya, Muluvay under provincial governors (Pradhani).
Amara-Nayaka System
Military commanders (Nayakas) governed territories, collected taxes and maintained armies.
Nayakas of Madurai and Thanjavur became semi-independent post-Talikota (1565 CE).
Council of Ministers
Assisted king in governance; included Mahapradhani (chief minister), Dalavay (commander).
Krishnadevaraya’s council managed daily administration, as noted in Amuktamalyada.
Local Governance
Village assemblies managed local affairs; temples as administrative hubs.
Hampi inscriptions show village-level tax collection.

elements.text: Nayankara and Amaram systems

The Nayankara and Amaram systems were the administrative and military backbone of the Vijayanagara Empire, facilitating imperial control over a vast and diverse macro-region. Together, they functioned as a decentralized mechanism to manage vast territories, secure steady revenue, and maintain a formidable army across the south.
The Nayankara System
The Nayankara system centered on military chiefs or elite warriors known as Nayakas.

rows.text: Role of the Nayakas

Most Nayakas were Telugu warriors who acted as territorial magnates or agents of the central government (Rayas). They held command over outlying territories and served as vital intermediaries, particularly in the Tamil country
Administrative Functions
Beyond military duties, some Nayakas served as Durga Dannaiks (fortress commanders) or provincial governors to enhance central control
Central Authority
The system was not originally hereditary; the King (overlord) held the prerogative to revoke or change Nayankara assignments to prevent chiefs from building independent power bases
Evolution

Before the Battle of Talikota (1565 CE), Nayakas were largely dependent on the rulers. Afterward, the system fragmented, leading to the rise of semi-independent Nayak kingdoms like those in Senji, Tanjore, and Madurai

elements.text: The Amaram System
The Amaram system was the land-tenure component of the Nayankara structure, where land was assigned to chiefs in lieu of cash salaries.

rows.text: Nature of Tenure
Land parcels known as Amaram were granted to Nayakas. Holders did not own the land but enjoyed revenue rights over its income.
Extent
It is estimated that approx 75% (three-fourths) of all villages in the empire were under Amaram tenure.
Reciprocal Obligations

In exchange for these revenue rights, Nayakas were required to:
• Maintain a specified body of troops and horses for the King's military needs.
• Make annual revenue payments and provide lavish gifts to the monarch on special occasions, such as the Mahanavami festival.
• Invest in local development, such as repairing irrigation tanks, reclaiming wasteland, and patronizing temples

elements.text: Interpretations of the nature of the Nayankara and Amaram Systems
The Nayankara and Amaram systems have been subject to various historiographical interpretations, ranging from a decentralized feudal structure to a symbolic segmentary state.
• Feudal Model: Some scholars view the system as a form of feudalism, citing the payment of tribute and rendering of

military service as key indicators.
• Administrative Office: Historians like D.C. Sircar and T.V. Mahalingam argue it was an administrative device where

Nayakas were warriors holding an office (kara) rather than autonomous lords.
• Military Office: A prominent view is that it was an administrative office (kara) bestowed on the condition of military

service rather than a purely feudal land right
• Segmentary State: Burton Stein characterizes it as a segmentary state, where the king held "ritual sovereignty" while

Nayakas exercised actual political control in the peripheral regions.
• War State: N.K.Sarkar viewed the Militaristic model of Vijaynagara as an empire that functioned as a confederacy of

chieftains cooperating under a strong leader to maintain a perpetual war footing .
• Inspiration: The system is believed to have been influenced by the Iqta system of the Delhi Sultanate, particularly in its
use of revenue assignments to maintain standing forces.
2. Socio-Economic Organisation of the Vijayanagara Empire

The Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) was characterized by a sophisticated socio-economic structure that integrated advanced agricultural practices, global maritime trade, and a pluralistic social hierarchy.

rows.text: Agrarian System & Revenue
The economy relied on diverse crops and state-led expansion into virgin soils. The Athavane (Revenue Dept.) assessed land tax based on soil quality, typically amounting to 1/6th of produce.
• Rice (black and white varieties), cotton, sugarcane, and spices like pepper were staples.
Infrastructure & Land Tenure
Aggressive investment in hydraulic engineering countered the semi-arid Deccan climate. Land was categorized into Amara (military), Bhandaravada (crown), and Manya (tax-free). |

• Infrastructure: Construction of the Kamalapura Tank and Tungabhadra canals.
• Tenures: Amara (military assignments for Nayakas), Bhandaravada (crown lands), and Manya (tax-free)
Trade, Industry & Currency

As "Lords of the Eastern and Western Oceans," rulers dominated maritime trade. Production flourished across textile, metal, and mining sectors, supported by prestigious gold coins featuring Hindu iconography.

• Trade Hubs: Pulicat (textile export) and Bhatkal (horse imports)
• Wealth: Gold Varahas (Pagodas) were traded globally.
Social Structure
A varna-based society where Brahmins (Telugu Niyogis) held secular political and military offices, featuring a respectable status for women. But Sati, Devadasi, and child marriage also existed.
• Gangadevi authored the Sanskrit epic Madhuravijayam.
Temple Economy
Temples operated as central socio-economic hubs, and professional corporations organized economic activities.
• The Srirangam Temple employed hundreds and loaned money to peasants.
Urbanization & Pluralism
Built on decentralized Amara-Nayaka and Ayagar systems, the empire's wealth created a "Golden Age" marked by high religious tolerance and massive urban centers.

• Hampi housed approx 250,000 to 480,000 residents by the 16th century.
• Rulers built mosques for Muslim soldiers and patronized Jain establishments like Shravanabelagola.

elements.text: Reasons for Economic Prosperity of Hampi

rows.text: Agrarian Excellence & Irrigation

• Water Management: Deva Raya I pioneered massive dams across the Tungabhadra and Haridra rivers; built the Kamalapura Tank to combat the semi-arid Deccan climate.
• Crop Variety: Encouraged high-value cash crops (cotton, sugarcane, spices) alongside rice.
• Geopolitical Assets: Seizure of the fertile Raichur Doab (Krishna-Tungabhadra interfluve) heavily boosted grain production.
Thriving Trade & Commerce

• Global Links: Dominated maritime routes via Malabar/Coromandel coasts; exported rice, fine textiles, iron, and spices to Persia, Arabia, and China.
• Strategic Imports: Prioritized high-quality Arabian/Persian war horses for the imperial cavalry, alongside luxury silks and pearls.
• Traveler Accounts: Nicolo de Conti and Domingo Paes documented Hampi's bustling bazaars packed with international merchandise and precious gems.
Efficient Taxation & Wealth

• The Athavane: A highly sophisticated central revenue department.
• The Sist (Land Tax): Levied based on soil classification (wet, dry, orchard), generally fixed at one-sixth of the total produce.
• Monetization: Issued high-prestige gold Varahas (Pagodas) featuring Hindu deities; Paes praised them as "the most beautiful in the world."
Mining & Skilled Industries

• Diamond Hubs: Exploited world-famous diamond fields like the Kollur mine (source of the legendary Koh-i-Noor).
• Manufacturing: Highly specialized textile weaving and silk clusters produced exports for markets as far as Persia.
• Artisanal Guilds: Organized bodies of blacksmiths, sculptors, and weavers maintained rigid quality controls.
Territorial Stability

• Military Dominance: Rulers like Krishnadevaraya secured frontiers, providing a peaceful environment for commerce.
• Amara-Nayaka System: Military commanders governed territories and collected taxes, ensuring decentralized stability and rapid troop mobilization.
• Traveler Account: Persian envoy Abdur Razzaq recorded the empire's formidable seven-line fortifications and the prosperity of its major trade ports like Calicut.

elements.text: 3. Art, Architecture and Literature
A. Art

rows.text: Sculpture
Characterized by intricate carvings of gods, warriors, and animals on temple pillars and monolithic statues
Ugra Narasimha Statue (Hampi), fierce expressions and intricate details.
Reliefs & Frescoes
Bas-reliefs depicting religious and royal themes. Murals and frescoes, though fewer in number, were found in temple ceilings.
Virupaksha Temple Frescoes – Ceiling paintings depicting scenes from Ramayana and Mahabharata
Metalwork & Bronze Art
Skilled bronze casting influenced by Chola traditions → used for religious and royal idols.
Vijayanagara Bronze Idols – life-size statue of Krishnadevaraya and his queens, Tirumalamba and Chinnadevi.
Dance & Music
With royal patronage, temples served as cultural centres for Bharatanatyam and Carnatic music.
Purandara Dasa (father of Carnatic music) received patronage from Krishnadeva Raya.
Yakshagana & Theater
A form of traditional storytelling involving music, dance, and dialogues, popular in Karnataka during Vijayanagara rule.
Yakshagana Performances – Based on Puranic tales; performed in open-air theatres.

elements.text: B. Temple Architecture

The architectural evolution of the Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) reflects a grand synthesis of regional South Indian traditions and contemporary Indo-Islamic influences from the Deccan Sultanates, creating a unique imperial style that dominated the southern peninsula for over two centuries.
I. Evolution of the Architectural Style

The architectural evolution of the Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE) is a grand synthesis of earlier South Indian traditions, including Chola, Pandya, Hoysala, and Chalukya elements, interwoven with distinctive Indo-Islamic features.

rows.text: Early Phase (Sangama)

• Initially relied on regional patterns from the Deccan and focused on reviving traditional Dravidian styles by building upon older foundations.
• Expansion of the Virupaksha Temple (Hampi): Builders added to an ancient, pre-existing sacred site, incorporating earlier Chalukyan layouts into the growing Dravidian imperial style.
Peak Phase (Tuluva)

• Under Krishnadevaraya, the style reached its zenith, characterized by massive temple enclosures, elaborate mandapas, and towering gateways that emulated Chola grandeur.
• Vittalaswami Temple (Hampi): The pinnacle of Vijayanagara stonework, known for its iconic stone chariot and musical pillars.
Synthesis Phase

• As the empire expanded and engaged with neighboring Deccan Sultanates, courtly and secular architecture integrated Indo-Islamic elements like arches, domes, and vaults alongside traditional Hindu features.
• Lotus Mahal (Hampi): A two-story pavilion designed with mixed architectural forms, including Indo-Islamic arches, likely intended for royal councils.

elements.text: II. Distinctive Architectural Features

rows.text: Rayagopuram
Monumental, towering entrance gateways that often dwarfed the central sanctums, serving as powerful symbols of royal and spiritual authority.
The towering southern gateway of the Virupaksha Temple or the massive gopuram at Chidambaram.
Pillared Kalyana Mandapa
Highly ornate, open pavilions with intricately carved pillars, often featuring Yali motifs (mythical beasts), deities, and musicians, used for divine marriage ceremonies.
The Kalyana Mandapa within the Vittala Temple enclosure.
Monolithic Sculptures
Massive figures carved directly from natural rock outcrops.
The 6.7-meter-tall Ugra Narasimha and the Sasivekalu Ganesha.
Secular Indo-Islamic Structures
Palaces and utility buildings that utilized arches and domes borrowed from neighboring Sultanates.
The Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, and Queen’s Bath.
Material Transition
A deliberate shift to local, rigid hard granite to ensure greater structural longevity and scale.
The departure from the soft soapstone (chloritic schist) favored by the earlier Hoysalas.
Civil Works
Advanced hydraulic engineering designed for water storage and transport.
The Kamalapura Tank and the Tungabhadra Canal system.
Engineering Marvels
Solid stone pillars designed with advanced acoustic properties that produce clear musical resonant sounds.
The musical pillars at Vittala Temple.

elements.text: III. Impact and Historical Significance

The Vijayanagara era (14th–17th centuries) revolutionized Indian architecture by harmonizing diverse regional elements, blending Southern Dravidian styles with Northern and Indo-Islamic features. This synthesis birthed the ornate Provida style and influenced subsequent generations of builders.

rows.text: Cultural Syncretism
Successfully integrated centuries-old Dravidian temple architecture with Islamic structural elements.
The adoption of arches, domes, and mortar to form a "cultural mosaic".
Symbol of Sovereignty
Served as a powerful physical representation of political and spiritual authority.
Monumental Gopurams towering above temples to signify royal might.
Advanced City Planning
Featured an organized, highly fortified grid designed to facilitate thriving international trade networks.
The fortified grid of bazaars, pavilions, and sacred centers in Hampi.
Water Management
Demonstrated exceptional engineering prowess by constructing large-scale water routing and storage networks.
Massive irrigation systems, the Tungabhadra Dam, and elaborate pushkarnis (stepped tanks).
Hard Stone Preference
Transformed regional construction techniques and structural scale by breaking away from softer stones.
A deliberate transition from soft soapstone to durable local granite, paired with intricate stucco work.
Foundation for Later Eras
Laid down the core aesthetic and structural blueprint for subsequent ruling lineages.
Influenced the building styles of the later Nayak kingdoms of Madurai, Tanjore, and Senji.
Global Recognition
It stands as an internationally celebrated architectural landscape and one of the largest open-air archaeological ruins in the world.
The sprawling ruins of the capital city, Hampi, designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

elements.text: C. Literature

rows.text: Multilingual Literary Patronage
The Vijayanagara rulers encouraged literature in Sanskrit, Kannada, Telugu, and Tamil.
Krishnadevaraya patronised court poets; composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu.
Sanskrit Literature
Flourished under royal patronage; many works focused on religion, dharma, and poetry.
Madhava Vidyaranya wrote Sarvadarshana Samgraha
Kannada Literature
Witnessed significant growth; addressed history, devotion, and philosophy.
Chamarasa wrote Prabhulinga Leele → a spiritual biography of the 12th-century saint Allama Prabhu.
Telugu Literature
Reached new heights during the reign of Krishnadevaraya; many poets flourished.
Allasani Peddana, Andhra Kavita Pitamaha (Father of Telugu Poetry), wrote Manucharitram.
Religious and Bhakti Literature
Many works were inspired by Hinduism and the Bhakti movement, emphasizing devotion to deities.
Kanakadasa and Purandaradasa composed devotional songs in Kannada that influenced Carnatic music.
Historical and Political Writings
Writings focused on the greatness of the Vijayanagara Empire, its kings, and its military exploits.
Raya Vachakam, a Telugu work, describes Krishnadevaraya’s military achievements.
Foreign Accounts
Foreign travellers documented the literary and cultural richness of the empire.
Duarte Barbosa and Abdur Razzaq noted the extensive use of Kannada and Telugu as the primary languages of the land.
