Influenced by Greco-Roman style; realistic and Hellenistic features.
Wavy hair, Roman toga-like robes, and calm expressions. Found in Taxila and Peshawar region.
Bodhisattva Images
Especially prominent in Mahayana art; emphasis on compassion and salvation.
Bodhisattva Padmapani and Avalokiteshvara murals in Ajanta.
Mudras (Gestures)
Symbolic hand gestures used in Buddha images to convey different teachings.
Abhaya Mudra (fearlessness), Dharmachakra Mudra (turning the wheel of law), Dhyana Mudra.

elements.text: 4. Buddhist Stupa Architecture
The Buddhist stupa transcends architecture, symbolizing the Buddha as the Emperor of the Spiritual Universe.

elements.caption: Diagram: parts of a Buddhist stupa

elements.text: Fig. Parts of Sanchi Stupa

rows.text: Anda (Dome)
Hemispherical mound symbolizing the universe or the cosmic mountain (Mt. Meru); houses relics.
Sanchi Stupa (MP) – solid brick and stone hemispherical dome
Harmika
The square railing on top of the dome represents the heaven of gods.
Sanchi – indicating a sacred enclosure.
Chhatra (Umbrella)
Triple-tiered parasol above the harmika denoting the Triratna (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha); Axis Mundi Concept: cosmic axis connecting heaven and earth.
Sanchi Stupa – representing spiritual sovereignty
Vedika (Railing)
Stone railing enclosing the stupa; demarcates sacred space; often intricately carved.
Bharhut and Sanchi – depict Jataka tales and scenes from Buddha’s life.
Torana (Gateway)
Monumental gateways in four cardinal directions; richly decorated with reliefs.
Sanchi Toranas – show events like Buddha’s birth, enlightenment, etc.
Medhi (Terrace)
Circular Platform above base; supports the large hemispherical dome (anda)
Amaravati Stupa – multiple terraces and elaborate decoration.
Pradakshina Patha
Circumambulatory path around the stupa; promotes meditative walking worship.
Sanchi and Amaravati
Material and Evolution
Initially made of brick (Mauryan period), later stone; evolved in size, ornamentation, and symbolism.
Ashokan stupas – brick; Sanchi (later phase) – stone with sculptural enhancements.

elements.text: Other Buddhist Architecture

rows.text: Chaitya Griha (Prayer Hall)
Rock-cut or structural hall with a stupa at the end for congregational worship; features barrel-vaulted roof and colonnaded aisles.
Karle Chaitya (Maharashtra) – 2nd CE; elaborately carved pillars
Viharas (Monastic Residences)
Used as living quarters for monks; initially simple cells, later evolved into complex layouts with halls and cells.
Ajanta Caves – Cave 1, 2, 16, 17 – serve as viharas with exquisite murals and structural planning.
Multi-functional Spaces
Later viharas included prayer halls, cells, lecture spaces, and even libraries.
Ellora Caves (Cave 5) – long hall with benches (possible lecture hall).
Apse Design
Semi-circular rear end of the hall, often housing the stupa; allows for ritual circumambulation.
Bhaja Chaitya (1st century BCE) – early example with horseshoe-shaped apse.
Wooden Imitation in Stone
Architectural elements like beams and ribs were carved in stone to imitate earlier wooden construction.
Karle and Bhaja Caves – stone ribs in the ceiling replicate wooden forms.
Elaborate Facades and Sculptures
Ornamented with intricate carvings, reliefs, and figures from Buddhist iconography.
Ajanta and Ellora – Buddha figures, Bodhisattvas, floral motifs, mythical beings.
Integration with Paintings
Architectural elements often seamlessly integrate with painting and sculpture.
Ajanta Cave 1 & 2 – a fusion of painted murals with structural features.
Adaptation to Landscape
Carved into a hillside or rock face, making use of natural contours for design.
Nasik Caves – strategically cut into rock faces above the river to offer serenity.

elements.text: 5. Factors that led to the Decline of Buddhism in India
The decline of Buddhism in India was not a sudden collapse but a gradual process influenced by internal institutional shifts, religious competition, and external shocks.

rows.text: Internal Decadence
Fragmentation into splinter groups (Mahayana, Vajrayana) compromised the original, simple teachings of the Buddha.
The adoption of Tantric practices in the Vajrayana phase alienated the non-monastic(household) followers.
Linguistic Alienation
Shifting from vernacular Pali/Prakrit to elite Sanskrit created a severe communication barrier with the masses.
Abandoning local dialects alienated Buddhism's primary, egalitarian social base.
Religious Absorption
The Bhakti movement and Puranic Hinduism dynamically countered and absorbed Buddhist philosophy.
The assimilation of the Buddha into Hinduism as the ninth avatar of Vishnu made a distinct Buddhist identity redundant.
Loss of Royal Patronage
State support dried up after Harshavardhana, while rival dynasties actively revived Vedic traditions.
The Shungas and Guptas heavily patronized Brahmanism, leaving the Sangha financially vulnerable.
Social Realignment
Traditional support bases among the mercantile and artisan classes shifted their religious allegiances over time.
Some historians argue that changing patronage patterns and conversions in eastern India contributed to Buddhism's decline.
Persecution & Hostility
Selective hostility from regional rulers disrupted monastic peace and challenged Buddhist survival.
Textual traditions such as the Divyavadana accuse Pushyamitra Shunga of persecuting Buddhists, but modern historians consider the evidence inconclusive.
External Invasions
Violent foreign incursions physically liquidated monastic centres, dealing terminal blows to the religion's infrastructure.
Huna chiefs (Mihirakula) devastated northwestern centres; Bakhtiyar Khalji famously sacked Nalanda University (c. 1200 CE).

elements.text: 6. Contemporary Relevance of Buddhist Ideals

Buddhism provides a timeless framework for addressing modern global crises, ranging from mental health to ethical governance and environmental sustainability. Its core philosophies offer a pragmatic path to social and individual well-being that remains highly relevant in the 21st century.

rows.text: Mental Health & Mindfulness
The Eightfold Path's focus on Right Mindfulness (Samyak Smriti) is widely used to counter digital burnout and anxiety.
Vipassana and Zen meditation are integrated into corporate and clinical programs to improve cognitive focus.
Environmental Ethics
The Middle Path (Madhyamika) promotes moderation and the interconnectedness of all beings, prefiguring modern sustainability.
Buddhist monastic rules against cutting trees align with modern community-based forest management and India’s Mission LiFE.
Ethical Governance
Ashoka’s Dhamma provides a model for servant leadership, prioritizing the welfare (Praja-Hita) and happiness of the collective over state power.
Modern anti-corruption bodies like Lokpal mirror the oversight roles of ancient Dhamma Mahamatras.
Social Justice & Reform
The Buddhist rejection of varna and caste hierarchies continues to inspire egalitarian movements for human dignity.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s revival of Navayana Buddhism empowered marginalized communities to fight systemic discrimination.
Soft Power & Diplomacy
India utilizes its status as the birthplace of Buddhism to anchor its Act East Policy and strengthen strategic ties in South and Southeast Asia.
The Buddhist Tourism Circuit and Nalanda University revival project serve as tools for cultural diplomacy.
Conflict Resolution
Principles of non-violence (Ahimsa) and compassion (Karuna) provide a blueprint for peaceful dialogue and restorative justice.
Ashoka's landmark shift from military victory (Bherighosha) to moral conquest (Dhammaghosha) brands India as a non-aggressive global power.
Scientific Temper
The emphasis on rational inquiry and the cessation of suffering through evidence-based practice facilitates a modern spirit of skepticism and experimentation.
Early Buddhist skepticism toward religious dogmas parallels contemporary scientific and logical traditions.
National Identity
Buddhist iconography forms the bedrock of India's state symbols, representing the nation's historical continuity and values.
The Sarnath Lion Capital is the National Emblem, and the Ashoka Chakra is featured on the National Flag

elements.text: Buddhism’s egalitarian ideals, missionary zeal, and cultural patronage significantly influenced Asia. Though it later declined in India, its legacy endures through art, literature, and global spiritual relevance.
Jainism

Jainism, emerging in the 6th century BCE, challenged Vedic rituals with its focus on non-violence and asceticism. Led by 24 Tirthankaras, it thrived prominently in India until around the 13th century CE, after which it declined in mainland influence but persisted in regional strongholds, shaping India’s spiritual and artistic landscape.
1. Core Teachings and Philosophy

rows.text: Pancha Mahavratas
Five vows: Ahimsa (non-violence), Satya (truth), Asteya (non-stealing), Aparigraha (non-possession), Brahmacharya (celibacy).
Path to liberation for monks.
Mahavira added Brahmacharya to Parsvanatha’s four.
Ratnatraya
Three jewels: Right Belief, Right Knowledge, and Right Action.
Guide to Moksha.
Tattvartha Sutra systematically explains Ratnatraya.
Anekantavada
Reality has multiple perspectives; truth is relative.
Promotes tolerance.
Syadvada’s “maybe” logic.
Soul & Moksha
Soul (Jiva) is trapped by Karma; liberation through penance frees it.
Jiva vs. Ajiva (matter).
Jīva is inherently pure, eternal, and omniscient.
Rejects Vedic authority
World runs on eternal laws, not a supreme deity
Self-reliance for salvation.
Rejected Vedic rituals, emphasizing individual spiritual effort (self-realization).

elements.text: 2. Jain Literature

rows.text: Scriptural Division
Divided into canonical (Agamic) and non-canonical (non-Agamic) texts.
Agamas (Svetambara), Shatkhandagama, Kasayapahuda (Digambara).
Language of Literature
Early texts written in Prakrit dialects (especially Ardha-Magadhi), later in Sanskrit, Apabhramsha, Tamil, and Kannada.
Tattvartha Sutra (Sanskrit), Samayasara (Prakrit), Jain Puranas in Kannada.
Sects and Textual Canon
Svetambara and Digambara sects have different canons due to doctrinal differences.
Svetambara: Acaranga Sutra, Sutrakritanga Digambara: Shatkhandagama, Kasayapahuda
Doctrinal Content
Focuses on ethics, cosmology, karma theory, metaphysics, conduct for monks and laity, and stories of Tirthankaras.
Tattvartha Sutra, Samayasara, Ratnakaranda Sravakachara.
Fourfold Division of Non-Canonical Texts (Anuyogas)
Digambaras classify literature based on themes: Pratham, Charan, Karan, and Dravya Anuyoga.
Padma Purana (Pratham), Mulachara (Charan), Tiloyapannatti (Karan), Samayasara (Dravya)
Commentarial Tradition
Jain scholars wrote extensive commentaries and digest works to preserve and interpret original texts.
Sarvarthasiddhi by Pujyapada (on Tattvartha Sutra), Niyamsara by Kundakunda
Narrative and Didactic Works
Use of legends, parables, and universal history to convey ethical teachings.
Adi Purana, Uttara Purana, Lilavati Saram
Biographical Literature
Chronicles the lives of Tirthankaras, saints, and illustrious devotees.
Kalpa Sutra (Bhadrabahu), Vasudevahindi, Charitras
Preservation of Ancient Knowledge
Jain texts contributed to grammar, poetics, mathematics, astronomy, and biographies of ancient rulers and saints.
Gommatsara, Tiloyapannatti (cosmology), Parishishtaparvan by Hemachandra.
Moral & Ethical Focus
Emphasis on non-violence, asceticism, detachment, and soul purification.
Acaranga Sutra (code of conduct), Ratnakaranda Sravakachara
Gender and Inclusivity
Some texts highlight the spiritual equality of women, though interpretations vary between sects.
Stories of Jain nuns and the role of women in Kalpa Sutra.

elements.text: 3. Jain Art and Architecture

rows.text: Emphasis on Simplicity and Symbolism
Simple meditation cells in Udayagiri-Khandagiri Caves, Dilwara Temples
Austere design, reflecting the ideals of renunciation, non-violence, and spiritual elevation.
Rock-Cut Caves
Udayagiri-Khandagiri Caves (Odisha), Ellora Jain caves (9th–10th CE, Maharashtra).
One of the earliest forms, during the Mauryan and post-Mauryan periods. Used as monastic dwellings and prayer halls.
Stupa Architecture
Mathura Jain Stupa, Kankali Tila Stupa, with railings and narrative sculptures.
Jain stupas are similar to Buddhist ones but often have images of Tirthankaras and were used to house sacred relics.
Iconography of Tirthankaras
Bahubali statue at Shravanabelagola (Gommateshwara), sculptures of Rishabhanatha, Parshvanatha with snake hoods.
Jain art is known for detailed iconography of the 24 Tirthankaras, mostly depicted in kayotsarga (standing) or padmasana (seated) posture.
Temple Architecture – Early Phase
Deogarh Jain Temple (UP, Gupta period); Jain temples in Aihole, Badami (Karnataka).
Early Jain temples show simple design with emphasis on worship halls and sanctum, built under regional dynasties like Guptas, Chalukyas, and Rashtrakutas.
Temple Architecture – Later Phase
Dilwara Temples , Ranakpur Temple (15th CE), Khajuraho Jain temples (10th–12th CE).
Later temples show highly ornate carvings, elaborate mandapas, white marble or sandstone and richly decorated domes and ceilings.
Towers and Domes (Shikharas)
Shikharji Temples, Palitana Temples (Gujarat) with a cluster of shikharas
Often have multiple shikharas symbolizing ascent to moksha and feature toranas (gateways) and cloisters.
Pillared Halls and Mandapas
Dilwara Temples’ Lotus Ceiling, Ranakpur Temple’s 1,444 carved pillars, no two alike.
Jain temples include beautifully carved pillars with geometric and floral motifs, often with narrative panels and ceiling medallions.
Symbolism in Ornamentation
Lotus ceiling motifs, Ambika Yakshi statues, Siddhachakra diagrams in temple walls
Use of lotus, kalasha, svastika, serpents, and yakshas/yakshis to denote auspiciousness and spiritual values.
Manastambha (Pillars of Honor)
Manastambha at Shravanabelagola, Moodabidri, Kulpakji Temple
Erected in front of temples as a symbol of humility, indicating ego suppression before entering the divine space.
Regional Influence and Patronage
Chalukyas (Aihole), Rashtrakutas (Ellora), Solankis (Mount Abu), Hoysalas (Shravanabelagola), Pallavas (Sittanavasal)
Adapted to local styles – Dravidian, Nagara, and Vesara – and received patronage from multiple dynasties across India.
Pilgrimage Complexes on Hills
Shatrunjaya (Palitana), Sammed Shikharji, Girnar, Shravanabelagola
Temples were often built atop hills symbolizing spiritual elevation, forming large sacred complexes.

elements.text: Jainism, founded on ahimsa, anekantavada, and aparigraha by Mahavira (24th Tirthankara), emphasizes asceticism and karma theory, significantly influencing Indian ethics, ecology, and non-violent movements.
Foreign Travellers

Foreign travellers visited India across centuries for reasons like trade, religion, diplomacy, and curiosity, leaving behind accounts that illuminate India's history, culture, and society. Their visit spans from ancient times (circa 300 BCE) to the modern period (up to the 17th century).
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Assess the importance of the accounts of the Chinese and Arab travellers in the reconstruction of the history of India. (2018)
1. Ancient India Travellers (300 BCE – 700 CE)
Travellers from Greece and China visited during the Mauryan, Gupta, and post-Gupta periods.
Significance of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Provides timelines missing in Indian sources.
Megasthenes’ Indika confirms Chandragupta Maurya’s reign (302-298 BCE).
Political Insights
Details administrative systems.
Hsuan Tsang describes Harsha’s land-grant system (630-645 CE).
Socio-Cultural Insights
Glimpses into caste and daily life.
Fa Hsien notes the plight of chandalas in Gupta society (405-411 CE).
Religious Exchange
Documents the spread of Buddhism.
Hsuan Tsang’s Si-Yu-Ki highlights Nalanda’s prominence.
Trade and Economy
Highlights trade routes and economic activities.
Ptolemy’s Geography maps Indian ports (130 CE).

elements.text: Limitations of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Relies on secondary sources, leading to inaccuracies.
Megasthenes’ claim of "no slavery" contradicts Kautilya’s Arthashastra.
Political Insights
Focuses on elites, neglecting commoners.
Megasthenes ignores rural Mauryan administration.
Socio-Cultural Insights
Misinterpretations due to cultural bias.
Megasthenes lists seven castes, confusing them with occupations.
Religious Exchange
Exaggerations lack archaeological corroboration.
Hsuan Tsang’s claim of 10,000 monks at Nalanda is unverified.
Trade and Economy
Limited depth in economic analysis.
Fa Hsien mentions cowries but lacks context on trade decline.

elements.text: 2. Medieval India Travellers (700 CE – 1500 CE)
Travellers from Arab, Persian, and European regions visited during the Delhi Sultanate and Vijayanagara periods.
Significance of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Chronicles dynasties and political events.
Ibn Battuta’s Rihla details Muhammad bin Tughluq’s reign (1333-1347 CE).
Political Insights
Reveals governance structures.
Abdur Razzaq describes Vijayanagara’s fortifications (1442-1445 CE).
Socio-Cultural Insights
Captures customs and traditions.
Marco Polo notes Southern India’s trade (1292-1294 CE).
Religious Exchange
Highlights religious tolerance.
Al-Masudi’s Meadows of Gold praises Gujarat’s rulers (957 CE).
Trade and Economy
Documents commercial prosperity.
Abdur Razzaq praises Calicut’s spice trade (1442 CE).

elements.text: Limitations of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Contains chronology errors.
Ibn Battuta’s vague "60 days in Multan" lacks precision.
Political Insights
Elite-centric, ignoring common governance.
Al-Biruni focuses on Mahmud of Ghazni’s court (1024-1030 CE).
Socio-Cultural Insights
Cultural prejudice affects objectivity.
Al-Biruni calls Indians "insular."
Trade and Economy
Language barriers lead to inaccuracies.
Arab references to "Mount Juran" remain unidentified.

elements.text: 3. Modern India Travellers (1500 CE – 1700 CE)
European travellers visited during the Mughal and Vijayanagara periods.
Significance of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Records political shifts and transitions.
Bernier’s Travels covers Aurangzeb’s reign (1658-1669 CE).
Political Insights
Details administrative structures.
Sir Thomas Roe describes Jahangir’s court (1615-1619 CE).
Socio-Cultural Insights
Offers cross-cultural comparisons.
Nuniz notes Vijayanagara women’s freedom (1535-1537 CE).
Religious Exchange
Comments on religious practices.
Barbosa details Kerala’s caste system (1500 CE).
Trade and Economy
Highlights India’s economic wealth.
Tavernier discusses India’s diamond mines (1638-1668 CE).

elements.text: Limitations of Their Accounts

rows.text: Historical Documentation
Focuses on extraordinary events like wars and decline, often neglecting day-to-day governance and historical continuity.
Bernier overemphasizes Mughal decline, ignoring administrative stability.
Political Insights
Shows a Eurocentric bias, misunderstanding Asian political systems, and overlooking regional powers and indigenous governance mechanisms.
Sir Thomas Roe major focus on Mughals.
Socio-Cultural Insights
Contains ethnocentric judgments and stereotypes, reducing complex cultures to simplistic and negative descriptions.
Manucci describes Indian customs as "barbarous" (1653–1708 CE), showing cultural bias.
Religious Exchange
Oversimplifies India’s diverse religious practices, social norms, and caste structures due to limited understanding.
Barbosa reduces complex caste hierarchies to just four, missing regional and occupational diversity.
Trade and Economy
Focused heavily on luxury goods, neglecting agrarian economies, rural markets, and internal trade mechanisms.
Tavernier highlights diamond trade but ignores agriculture, which was the economic backbone of India.

elements.text: Travellers by Origin
1. Greek Travellers

headers: Importance of Reconstruction in Indian History

rows.text: Megasthenes
Establishes Mauryan chronology and administration. Example: Indika describes Pataliputra’s layout and army of 400,000.
Deimachus
3rd BCE
Supplements Mauryan history under Bindusara. Example: Corroborates Megasthenes’ accounts.
Ptolemy
130 CE
Maps ancient India’s geography and trade. Example: Geography lists ports and commodities.

elements.text: Significance: Greek accounts provide the earliest external perspective, crucial for Mauryan history and trade networks.
2. Chinese Travellers

headers: Importance of Reconstruction in Indian History

rows.text: Fa Hsien
Documents Gupta society, Buddhism’s state, and trade hubs like Tamralipti. Example: Notes ‘chandalas’ and cowries as currency.
Hsuan Tsang

Details Harsha’s reign, Nalanda’s prominence, and feudalism. Visited the Pallava capital at Kanchipuram, and documented the Western Chalukyas of Badami. Example: Describes Kannauj assembly and land grants.
I-Tsing

Arrived via the maritime Spice Route to Tamralipti and spent nearly a decade studying and translating texts exclusively at Nalanda and Bodh Gaya. Example: Records precise account of the great Nalanda monastery in Bihar.

elements.text: Significance: Chinese accounts fill gaps in Buddhist history and socio-political transitions, especially during the Gupta and Harsha periods.
3. Arab & Persian Travellers

headers: Importance of Reconstruction in Indian History

rows.text: Al-Masudi
957 CE
Highlights Gujarat’s religious tolerance and maritime trade. Example: Meadows of Gold praises Bilahara Rajas.
Al-Biruni
Provides scientific and cultural insights during Ghaznavid invasions. Example: Tahqiq-i-Hind covers astronomy and castes.
Awfi
1220s CE
Records early Sultanate politics and trade. Example: Details Iltutmish’s relations with Khokhars and Caliph.
Ibn Battuta
Chronicles Delhi Sultanate’s administration and society. Example: Rihla details Tughluq’s court and postal system.
Abdur Razzaq
Describes Vijayanagara’s grandeur and Calicut’s trade. Example: Notes 300 harbours and Mahanavmi festival.

elements.text: Significance: Arab & Persian accounts offer a blend of political, cultural, and economic history, bridging Islamic and Indian traditions.
4. European & Russian Travellers

headers: Importance of Reconstruction in Indian History

rows.text: Marco Polo
Documents Southern India’s trade and rulers. Example: Notes Kakatiya and Pandyan prosperity.
Niccolò de’ Conti
Details Vijayanagara’s social customs. Example: Describes caste system and Sati practice.
Athanasius Nikitin
Records Bahmani Kingdom’s trade and customs. Example: Travels notes political conditions.
Duarte Barbosa
Chronicles Kerala and Vijayanagara’s society. Example: Details caste hierarchies.
Domingo Paes
Describes Vijayanagara’s peak under Krishnadeva Raya. Example: Notes city’s wealth and military.
Fernão Nuniz
Highlights Vijayanagara’s culture. Example: Records women’s role in astrology and wrestling.
Tavernier
Documents Mughal economy. Example: Details diamond mines and trade.
Bernier
Analyzes Mughal decline. Example: Travels critiques Aurangzeb’s policies.
Sir Thomas Roe
Offers Mughal court insights. Example: Describes Jahangir’s diplomacy.
Francois Bernier
Highlights the absence of a middle class in Mughal India, compares it with Europe’s socio-economic structures. Example: Notes “no middle state in India ”, only nobles and peasants.

elements.text: Foreign travellers’ accounts provide invaluable insights into India’s history, culture, and economy, but their biases, inaccuracies, and selective focus limit their reliability as sole historical sources.
Indian Philosophy
Indian philosophy, rooted in the Vedas and Upanishads, explores dharma, karma, and moksha through orthodox and heterodox schools, blending spirituality, logic, and ethics.
UPSC Mains PYQs
1. Indian philosophy and tradition played a significant role in conceiving and shaping the monuments and their art in India. Discuss. (2020)
Orthodox Schools (Āstika Darśanas)

rows.text: Nyāya (Founder - Gautama)

• Focuses on logic, reasoning, and epistemology
• Aims to remove ignorance through valid knowledge (pramāṇa)
• Views liberation (moksha) as a result of right knowledge
• 4 Pramāṇas: Perception (pratyakṣa), Inference (anumāna), Comparison (upamāna), Verbal testimony (śabda)

• Basis for Indian logic and debate traditions
• Used in ancient law courts and philosophical disputations.
Vaiśeṣika (Founder -Kanada)

• Closely allied with Nyāya
• Explains the universe through atomistic theory
• Believes all objects are composed of eternal atoms (paramāṇu)
• Liberation is through knowledge of reality
• 7 Padārthas: Substance, Quality, Motion, Generality, Particularity, Inherence, Non-existence

• Early form of physical science in Indian thought
• Influenced Ayurveda and cosmology.
Sāṅkhya (Founder - Kapila)

• Oldest philosophical system
• Dualistic: Reality is composed of Puruṣa (consciousness) and Prakṛti (matter)
• Liberation is separation of Puruṣa from Prakṛti

• 25 Tattvas (elements of reality)
• Satkāryavāda (effect pre-exists in cause)

• Influenced Bhagavad Gītā and classical Yoga
• Mentioned in Sāṅkhya Kārikā by Īśvarakṛṣṇa .
Yoga (Founder - Patanjali)

• Practical extension of Sāṅkhya
• Seeks mental and physical discipline for spiritual liberation
• Accepts the concept of a personal God (Īśvara)

• Aṣṭāṅga Yoga (Eight-limbed path): Yama, Niyama, Āsana, Prāṇāyāma, etc.
• Chitta-vṛtti-nirodha (control of mind)

• offers an antidote to modern distractions, stress, and fragmentation.
• Provides a framework for ethical living, mental clarity, and mind-body harmony.
Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (Founder - Jaimini)

• Emphasizes the ritualistic portion of the Vedas (karma-kāṇḍa)
• Believes in the authority of the Vedas but not in a creator God
• Liberation is achieved through the correct performance of rituals

• Apūrva: unseen force generated by rituals
• Śabda (verbal testimony) as the supreme source of knowledge

• Basis of Vedic ritualism
• Foundation for Dharmaśāstra and priestly duties in temples.
Vedānta (Uttara Mīmāṃsā) (Founder -Badarayana)

• Philosophical culmination of the Vedas and Upaniṣads
• Seeks knowledge of Brahman (Ultimate Reality)
• Three main sub-schools with differing views on the Brahman-Ātman relationship

• Advaita (Śaṅkara): Non-dualism
• Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Qualified non-dualism
• Dvaita (Madhva): Dualism

• Inspired Bhakti movements and temple-building (such as Śaṅkara temples, Rāmānuja’s Srivaishnavism)
• Based on Brahma Sūtras, Upaniṣads, Bhagavad Gītā

elements.text: Heterodox (Nāstika) Schools

rows.text: Cārvāka (Founder -Brihaspati)

• Materialist and atheistic school
• Rejected Vedas, afterlife, and liberation
• Advocated direct perception (pratyakṣa) as the only valid source of knowledge

• Lokāyata (worldly way)
• Hedonism: “Eat, drink, and be merry”
• No soul, no rebirth

• Critique of ritualism and Brahmanical orthodoxy
• Early Indian school of rationalism and skepticism.
Jainism (Founder -Mahavira (24th Tirthankara))

• Founded by Mahavira (6th century BCE)
• Atheistic but spiritual
• Believes in karma, rebirth, and liberation
• Emphasizes strict ethical conduct and asceticism

• Anekāntavāda (multi-faceted reality)
• Syādvāda (conditional perspective)
• Ahimsā (non-violence)

• Inspired temples at Mount Abu (Dilwara), Shravanabelagola (Gommateshwara statue)
• Influenced environmental and ethical movements.
Buddhism (Founder -Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha))

• Founded by Gautama Buddha (6th century BCE)
• Denies authority of Vedas and existence of a permanent self (anattā)
• Focuses on overcoming suffering through the Eightfold Path

• Four Noble Truths
• Eightfold Path
• Anicca (impermanence), Anattā (non-self), Dukkha (suffering)

• Inspired art like Sanchi Stupa, Ajanta murals
• Led to the development of Gandhara and Mathura schools of sculpture.
Ājīvika (Founder -Makkhali Gosala)

• Founded by Makkhali Gosāla (contemporary of Buddha and Mahavira)
• Accepted karma and rebirth but denied free will
• Believed in absolute determinism (niyati)

• Niyati (fate governs all)
• Rejected effort (purushārtha) as futile
• Fatalism and ascetic lifestyle

• Mentioned in Ashokan edicts (decline after the Mauryan era)
• Influenced early ascetic traditions
• Critiqued by both Jains and Buddhists.

elements.text: Role of Indian Philosophy in Monuments and Art

rows.text: Vedanta
Temples reflect Brahman’s unity and cosmic order, inspiring awe and devotion.
Chola temples (such as Brihadeeswara, 11th CE) embody Brahman in architecture.
Buddhism
Stupas and caves symbolize peace, meditation, and the Buddha’s path.
Sanchi Stupa (3rd BCE) mirrors the Four Noble Truths in its dome.
Jainism
Temples showcase intricate carvings, reflecting non-violence and the soul’s purity.
Dilwara Temples (11th-13th CE) depict Anekantavada in art.
Yoga/ Mimamsa
Ritual spaces in temples align with cosmic rhythms, aiding spiritual practice.
Thillai Nataraja Temple in Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu, is rich in yoga and cosmic symbolism.
Epics (Gita)
Sculptures narrate Dharma and Karma, teaching moral lessons visually.
Khajuraho panels (10th CE) depict Gita’s ideals.

elements.text: From Advaita’s oneness to Charvaka’s materialism, Indian philosophy’s diversity continues to inspire global thought on existence and liberation.
